title: 2D Shapes for Grade 2: Sides and Corners Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: 2D Shapes Grade 2: Sides and Corners + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Learn 2D shapes for Grade 2 by counting sides and corners. Name triangles to hexagons, sort by sides, spot flat shapes around you, and try a free quiz.
excerpt: A triangle has three corners, a hexagon has six — and once a Grade 2 child learns to count sides and corners, naming flat shapes stops being guesswork. Here is how to teach it, with a quick quiz to check the learning.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Draw a triangle on the board and ask a class of seven-year-olds how many corners it has, and you will hear two, three and four all at once. That little muddle is the whole reason 2D shapes at Grade 2 come down to two simple habits — counting the sides and counting the corners. Get a child fluent at those two counts and naming a triangle, a square or a hexagon stops being a memory game and becomes something they can work out for themselves.

A 2D shape is a flat shape. You can draw it on paper or trace it with a finger, but you cannot hold it in your hand the way you hold a ball or a box. In Grade 2 we stay firmly on these flat shapes — triangles, squares, rectangles, circles, pentagons and hexagons — and leave the solid shapes for later. Keeping that line clear saves a lot of confusion.

Sides and corners: the two things every 2D shape has

Here is the idea that makes 2D shapes for Grade 2 click into place. A side is a straight edge of the shape — one of the lines you would draw. A corner, which older children will later call a vertex, is the point where two sides meet. In my experience teaching this age, children get corners faster if you tell them to look for the pointy bits and touch each one with a finger while counting out loud.

Two rules do most of the work. First, in these shapes the number of sides and the number of corners is always the same — a shape with four sides has four corners. Second, the circle is the odd one out: it has no straight sides and no corners at all, just one smooth curve. That exception is worth pointing out on purpose, because a child who notices it really understands what a side is.

How to count without missing one

The classic mistake is counting the same corner twice or skipping the one you started on. Teach a simple fix: put a small pencil dot on the corner where you begin, then count your way around until you land back on the dot. The same trick works for sides. It feels slow at first, but it kills the guessing.

Naming the six shapes a Grade 2 child should know

Once counting is steady, naming follows almost by itself. A three-sided shape is a triangle. Four equal sides make a square; four sides with the long-short-long-short pattern make a rectangle. Five sides is a pentagon, six sides is a hexagon, and the curvy one with no corners is the circle. A quick tip that sticks: a honeycomb cell is a hexagon, and bees pack them together with no gaps — children remember six sides once they picture the bees.

Notice that the square and the rectangle share the same row. That is deliberate and it is honest — both have four sides and four corners. The difference is that a square’s four sides are all the same length, while a rectangle has two long sides and two short ones. I would not rush a child to explain that difference; let them feel it by comparing a square tile with a door.

Sorting shapes by number of sides

Counting and naming really lock in when a child has to sort. Cut out a mixed pile of paper shapes — some triangles, some squares, a few pentagons and hexagons — and ask the child to make groups. Sorting by the number of sides is the most useful rule at this age because it maps straight onto the names.

  • Put every three-sided shape together and check that each one is a triangle.
  • Group the four-sided shapes, then split that group into squares and rectangles by looking at side lengths.
  • Find the five-sided shapes and name them pentagons; do the same for six-sided hexagons.
  • Set the circle to one side on its own — it has no straight sides, so it does not fit any of the counting groups.

One honest caveat here. Turn a square so it balances on a corner and many children suddenly call it a diamond. It is not a different shape — it is the same square, just rotated. Show this on purpose. A shape keeps its name however you spin it, and spotting that is a real Grade 2 win.

Spotting 2D shapes in everyday objects

The best practice happens away from the worksheet. Flat shapes are hiding all over an Indian home, and a two-minute shape hunt makes the learning stick. The face of a clock and a ₹5 coin are circles. A slice of bread or a window pane is usually a rectangle. A warning road sign is a triangle. The Ashoka Chakra sits inside a circle, while a football is stitched from little pentagons and hexagons — point at one and count the sides together.

Ask your child to find three circles, three rectangles and one triangle before dinner. Because they have to count sides and corners to be sure, this game quietly drills the exact skill that matters, and it never feels like homework.

Try the quiz, then the printable worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly what we covered — counting sides and corners, naming the six shapes, and sorting them. Let your child answer, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for more written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 2 2D Shapes Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on sides, corners and shape names. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: How many sides does a triangle have?
questions.explanation: A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners. The name even starts with tri, meaning three.

questions.q: Which shape has no corners at all?
questions.explanation: A circle is one smooth curve with no straight sides and no corners. Every other shape here has corners.

questions.q: How many corners does a square have?
questions.explanation: A square has 4 sides, so it has 4 corners. The number of sides and corners is always the same.

questions.q: A shape has 6 sides. What is it called?
questions.explanation: Six sides make a hexagon. Think of a honeycomb cell, which the bees pack together.

questions.q: How many sides does a pentagon have?
questions.explanation: A pentagon has 5 sides and 5 corners.

questions.q: Which pair of shapes both have exactly 4 sides?
questions.explanation: A square and a rectangle both have 4 sides and 4 corners. A square has all sides equal; a rectangle has two long and two short.

questions.q: A clock face and a coin are the same 2D shape. Which one?
questions.explanation: Both are round with no corners, so both are circles.

questions.q: You turn a square so it balances on one corner. What shape is it now?
questions.explanation: It is still a square. A shape keeps its name when you turn it, even though it may look like a diamond.

faq.q: What 2D shapes should a Grade 2 child know?
faq.a: Six flat shapes: the circle, triangle, square, rectangle, pentagon and hexagon. For each one a child should be able to count the sides and corners and give the correct name.

faq.q: What is the difference between a side and a corner?
faq.a: A side is a straight edge of the shape — one of the lines you draw. A corner is the point where two sides meet. In these shapes the number of sides always equals the number of corners.

faq.q: Is a square the same as a rectangle?
faq.a: Both have 4 sides and 4 corners, so they are close cousins. The difference is that a square has all four sides equal, while a rectangle has two long sides and two short ones.

faq.q: Why does a circle have no corners?
faq.a: A circle is a single smooth curve with no straight sides. Corners only happen where two straight sides meet, and a circle has none, so it has zero corners.
